originalTitle: Mega datacentre planned for outer Melbourne will be six times bigger than a large shopping centre
summary: More than 3,600 people sign petition for careful assessment of proposed AI hub, now a flashpoint for national debate on datacentre boom
content: For some residents it started with a letter in the mailbox. It was a “friendly introduction from the team behind the Victorian AI hub”. “I am knocking on doors to explain what we have in mind and, most importantly, to listen,” the letter from Syncline Energy stated. “Construction won’t start for at least two-years while we complete the planning and environmental approvals.” For others, news of the project had already spread, through social media and news reports which sounded the alarm before the company had begun its communication efforts. The site for what has been dubbed a mega datacentre in Plumpton, around 30km north-west of the Melbourne CBD, is now an empty paddock next to Melbourne’s renewable energy hub, just off the Calder Freeway. It’s near a fast-growing suburb, transmission lines, and a stone’s throw from where Harry Houdini made what was claimed to be Australia’s first controlled powered flight in 1910. Planes from nearby Tullarmarine airport fly low overhead, and on weekends the sky is punctured by the lights and sounds of the Calder speedway. This paddock is rapidly becoming a microcosm of the growing community resentment to datacentres across Australia. The proposed site is 350 hectares, of which Syncline says 40% – 140ha, or just under six times the size of Chadstone shopping centre – will be used to house four datacentre buildings with maximum capacity of 2.4GW, with the remaining 60% to be open land. The proposed centre is larger than any currently operating in Australia and would consume more electricity than is generated by Victoria’s largest power station, Loy Yang A. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The sheer scale of the project has alarmed residents before shovels have hit the ground, building on a growing deep discomfort with the explosion in datacentre construction. An April report by lobby group Data Centres Australia said there were 30 datacentres in operation in Victoria, with another 30 in the pipeline. Environmental impacts, electricity and water use, concerns about the rise of AI more broadly, and the impact of campaigns in the US – which show developments stretching for miles, lit up like an international airport and with a constant hum of white noise and higher power prices – are feeding community concerns. A petition calling on the state government to “ensure the environmental, cultural, social and infrastructure implications of the proposed Victorian AI Hub are fully assessed and publicly considered,” as well as the cumulative effects of other new datacentres, has amassed over 3,600 signatures. It was started by Molly Walker, who lives over 250km away in the Grampians and first heard about the plans on TikTok. Walker, who works in conservation, said the scale of the project made her think “enough is enough”. “How much is being taken away from the environment?” she asked. “There’s also the noise … I’ve heard a lot about the datacentres in America and how much noise they produce. I did some research and found they’re not much different from the ones here in terms of the impact.” Other locals feel the western suburbs have become “a dumping ground”. “They always say they can’t put datacentres out in the east because of the land. The west has these vast lands and because of the socio-demographic areas [of the east] people there are likely to complain,” says Dr Karen Austria. Austria grew up in the area, and is an electrical engineer by training. She says locals are concerned the industrial development could lead to a drop in house prices. She also points to the fact the location is within a green wedge, which the state government has said should have its environmental, economic and cultural values protected. “Why are you putting this in our back yard?” she asks. “They’re promising to do community consultation … but everyone has got this one letter and they feel like they don’t know enough about it yet and the company needs to communicate more.” ‘Desirable’ scale Much of the community anger about the wave of datacentres in development has stemmed from a lack of community consultation, and through fast-track approval processes that skip the lengthy council review to go straight to the state government. The managing director of Syncline Energy, Phil Galloway, says the company is carefully consulting with locals before submitting the planned application for the Plumpton site. “The process starts with our direct neighbours and works out from there. The conversations will take at least a year,” he says. Ecological surveys and cultural heritage work is being undertaken parallel to the community discussions, Galloway says, adding that locals need to be shown there will be no noise, heat island, traffic, ecology issues or pollution, “which means careful engineering, architecture and urban planning”. “It would be insincere if we submitted a planning permit and then sought that input later,” he says. Galloway says the large scale of the project is all about building sovereign AI capability, and making efficient use of land, energy and water. The size of the land will allow buffers and green space between the buildings and residents. It’s also almost entirely under the Melbourne airport flight path, which means there are planning restrictions against using it for housing. The company is promising to use solar, wind and battery storage and provide additional transmission and grid stability. Galloway says it will also create local jobs, a community fund and walking and cycling paths. “That scale can only be delivered through a major precinct connecting into the main 500kV grid rather than piecemeal smaller datacentres in the suburbs and rural towns,” he says. “From a network stability point of view, it is desirable to concentrate the datacentre load at a strong point in the grid and install buffering equipment so to stabilise any IT load changes.” A Facebook group created in opposition to the project has more than 300 members. chineseTitle: 计划在墨尔本郊外建造的大型数据中心将比大型购物中心大六倍
chineseSummary: 超过 3,600 人签署了请愿书，要求仔细评估拟建的人工智能中心，该中心现已成为全国数据中心繁荣辩论的热点
chineseContent: 对于一些居民来说，一切都是从邮箱里的一封信开始的。这是“维多利亚人工智能中心背后的团队的友好介绍”。 Syncline Energy 在信中表示：“我正在挨家挨户地敲门，解释我们的想法，最重要的是倾听。” “在我们完成规划和环境审批之前，施工至少要两年才能开始。”对于其他人来说，该项目的消息已经通过社交媒体和新闻报道传播开来，这在公司开始沟通工作之前敲响了警钟。位于墨尔本中央商务区西北约 30 公里处的普兰普顿 (Plumpton) 被称为大型数据中心的场地现在是墨尔本可再生能源中心旁边的一个空围场，就在考尔德高速公路附近。这里靠近快速发展的郊区和输电线路，距离哈利·胡迪尼 (Harry Houdini) 于 1910 年进行澳大利亚首次受控动力飞行的地方仅一箭之遥。附近塔拉马林机场 (Tullarmarine airport) 的飞机在头顶低空飞行，周末考尔德高速公路的灯光和声音刺破天空。这个围场正在迅速成为澳大利亚各地社区对数据中心日益增长的不满的一个缩影。拟议的场地面积为 350 公顷，Syncline 表示其中 40%（140 公顷，即 Chadstone 购物中心面积的六倍以下）将用于容纳四个最大容量为 2.4GW 的数据中心建筑，其余 60% 为开放土地。拟议中的中心比澳大利亚目前运营的任何中心都要大，消耗的电力也比维多利亚州最大的 Loy Yang A 发电厂所产生的电力还要多。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
